findings.title: Denial cache can lock in a deny caused by a stale folder tree
findings.body: `Check` now persists a negative result in `permDenialCache` for 30s whenever `checkPermission` returns false. The fallback added above only re-reads *permissions* from the DB; the folder hierarchy used by `checkInheritedPermissions` is still served from `folderCache` (also 30s TTL, see `buildFolderTree`). So for the exact case this PR targets – a resource that was just created in a folder the user only has inherited access to, or a brand-new folder – the folder tree lookup misses, the check is denied even after the fresh DB permission read, and that deny is then cached for the full TTL. The user is blocked for up to 30s even though a re-read of folders would have allowed access. Either skip caching the denial when the decision depended on the folder tree, or invalidate/refresh the folder tree on the fallback path.

findings.title: Every non-cached denial triggers a full permission re-query and an unbounded cache entry
findings.body: The cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (DB query for basic role, teams and permissions) whenever the cached scope map does not grant the requested resource. Combined with a denial cache keyed by `(namespace, user, action, name, parentFolder)`, any sequence of checks over distinct resource names the user cannot access produces one DB permission query per distinct name, and one new cache entry per distinct name. For bulk authorization (e.g. checking many dashboards during a search) or for a caller passing arbitrary names, this is a significant DB-load amplification versus the previous behaviour (single cached scope map), and the local cache grows without bound until TTL expiry. Consider rate-limiting the re-query (e.g. a short "recently refreshed" marker per user+action) instead of re-querying on every miss.

findings.title: Denial cache key built by naive concatenation can collide between distinct resources
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` joins `action`, `name` and `parent` with single underscores without escaping. Since Grafana UIDs may contain underscores, distinct requests map to the same key: e.g. name=`a_b`/parent=`c` and name=`a`/parent=`b_c` both produce `...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. A cached deny for one resource therefore denies access to a different resource for up to the TTL (and, less harmfully, the key shares the `".perm_"` prefix space with `userPermCacheKey`, so a colliding key makes the permission cache entry undecodable). Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions, or hash the components; also note the key omits group/resource and relies solely on the derived action string.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric records a miss when the cache was actually hit
findings.body: When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeds but the cached scope map does not grant access, control falls through to line 137 and increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label `"false"` (miss), even though the permission cache was hit. Because the per-function metric increments were removed from `getUserPermissions`, this is now the only accounting point, so cache hit-rate dashboards will systematically under-report hits for denied checks and make the new caching behaviour impossible to evaluate.

findings.title: Denial-cache test does not actually verify the short-circuit
findings.body: In "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but the permission cache is seeded with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. *no* permission. With the default `fakeStore` (nil user permissions) the request would be denied even if the denial cache were never consulted, so the test passes whether or not the new short-circuit works. Seed the permission cache with `true` (and/or assert that the store was not called) so a regression that skips `permDenialCache` is detected.
